summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy is a criminal offence in Myanmar under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years' imprisonment. Police apply it alongside vague public-decency provisions, and authorities have used it to detain people who cannot satisfactorily account for their presence. The provision remained in active use as recently as 2018, when the HIV-positive LGBTI advocate Aung Myo Htut was charged under it.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has intensified. The National Unity Government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured. Human Rights Myanmar's June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in those deaths, and described militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws as endangering the right to life. Torture and sexual violence in detention are reported.

Transgender visitors face a separate layer of exposure. Myanmar does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity and no legal gender recognition procedure exists. Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act allows police to detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset, criminalises face covering with up to three months' imprisonment, and is applied specifically against transgender people, who also report police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion. A trans woman describing events in 2016 recounted arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night while police alleged sex work; in 2013 trans women in Mandalay were forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, an episode police called a public service.

There is no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised: couples can cohabit and hold ceremonial marriages without legal action, but those ceremonies carry no legal standing.

Care access is constrained by the same regime. Section 377 was identified in 2013 as hampering the country's HIV response, and gay men, particularly those living with HIV or AIDS, face stigmatisation. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights names LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.
tangentialFactors:
Expression around LGBT life is restricted. In January 2025 the junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions against their publishers.

The civil-society infrastructure a visitor might rely on for support is under pressure. The Organization Registration Law of October 2022 provides for prison terms where organisations fail to comply with registration requirements, and compulsory military service announced in February 2024 compounds the pressure. Research from January 2025 found that the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement.

Official hostility coexists with long-standing cultural visibility. Nat kadaws, traditional spirit mediums who are transgender women, have been publicly visible for decades, and same-sex couples have held ceremonies drawing national attention, including an unofficial wedding in 2014 that triggered a backlash from social conservatives demanding enforcement of the anti-homosexuality law. Visibility has not produced legal protection.

The June 2019 death by suicide of a young gay librarian, Kyaw Zin Win, after workplace harassment prompted the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission to call for enactment of anti-discrimination provisions, one of the few instances of the country's protection machinery responding to an anti-LGBT killing.
localsOnly:
Residents live without enforceable anti-discrimination protection, and the measures on the books are symbolic. The 2019 Child Rights Law carries a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms. The 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals and carry no legal penalties. Neither instrument alters the criminal liability residents face under Section 377, which applies regardless of consent or privacy.

Confidence in the state's protection machinery is low among LGBT residents themselves. The report 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found that 50% of LGBT respondents had no confidence in the legal system and more than 68% feared repercussions from reporting abuse to it.

The Kyaw Zin Win case shows what institutional response looks like when it comes. The young gay man, a librarian at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, died in June 2019 after sustained harassment and bullying from colleagues; more than 600 people attended his funeral and a rainbow flag was wrapped around his coffin. The university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission ran a separate inquiry and called for anti-discrimination provisions.

Everyday life for LGBT residents is shaped by the criminalisation and stigma: same-sex couples cohabit openly in Yangon and Mandalay, and ceremonial marriages are celebrated, but the informal tolerance does not extend to legal standing or to encounters with police after dark. Queers of Burma Alternative research from January 2025 records displacement and fear among queer people under conscription.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty attached to Section 377 is reported inconsistently across sources: several give up to 10 years' imprisonment, others give life imprisonment, and one gives both. Which sentence applies under which circumstances is not resolved by the available material.

Nothing in the available material addresses entry screening, visa rules, or checks on gender markers in passports or other travel documents at Myanmar's borders. Whether immigration authorities inspect documents for inconsistency with a traveller's presentation is not sourced.

Whether Section 377 has been charged against foreign visitors, or applied to conduct outside the country's territory, is not sourced. The same gap applies to the reach of the 2024 Conscription Law in respect of foreign nationals.

Enforcement frequency after 2024 is not sourced: the available counts of killings cover the period since February 2021, and no current figure for prosecutions under Section 377 or Section 35(c) is available. Practical access to legal representation, consular assistance, and HIV treatment for a non-resident is likewise not covered.
